title: Differential Behavior of Uncleaved gp160 Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1) Envelope (Env) Glycoproteins
summary: The envelope glycoprotein (Env) of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) plays important roles in viral entry by coordinating host-cell receptor recognition and membrane fusion. Env is synthesized as a homotrimeric precursor, gp160, which is cleaved into gp120 and gp41 subunits. Although the cleaved form of Env is required for fusion, uncleaved Env remains plentiful on the surface of HIV-1-infected cells. Previous studies have suggested that uncleaved Env is conformationally more flexible than the cleaved form making its dynamics important for understanding the broader structural landscape of HIV-1 Env. In this study, we employed microsecond-long all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the dynamics of two structures of uncleaved HIV-1 Env that have been previously assigned to the same conformational state. Our results reveal differences in their conformational behavior, including differences in collective motions, FRET distributions, and trimer symmetry. These findings provide molecular-level insight into the structural plasticity of uncleaved HIV-1 Env and highlight that different structures within the same conformational state can exhibit distinct dynamic behavior.

title: Rapid Host Plant Adaptation via Ectopic Gene Conversion in Plutellid Moths
summary: Herbivorous insects face an extraordinary challenge: the chemical defenses of their host plants are highly diverse, rapidly evolving, and largely unpredictable. How insects meet this challenge remains poorly understood. Here we show that ectopic gene conversion (EGC) has repeatedly driven the evolutionary diversification of glucosinolate sulfatases (GSSs), the key larval counteradaptation in plutellid moths to glucosinolate based defenses in cruciferous plants. Across seven plutellid species, enzyme assays with heterologously expressed GSSs and 21 glucosinolates revealed distinct activity profiles: GSSs from species with broad host ranges within glucosinolate-containing plants showed balanced activity across substrates, whereas GSSs from specialists displayed profiles biased toward the glucosinolate composition of their host plants. Comparative genomic analyses identified extensive conversion among duplicated genes, both historically across the clade and in contemporary Plutella armoraciae. In this originally monophagous species, EGC-mediated diversification of GSS enzymes coincides with the rapid inclusion of a new cruciferous host within <200 years, demonstrating the potential of EGC to drive host-range expansion on strikingly short evolutionary timescales. Structural modelling and molecular dynamics simulations further support functional shifts in GSS enzymes arising from EGC-derived sequence alterations. Together, these results demonstrate that EGC provides a powerful mechanism for fine tuning detoxification enzymes, enabling herbivorous insects to adapt to chemically diverse host plants despite constrained enzymatic toolkits.

title: Towards predictive ecological biogeography: Predicting vegetation type using fine-scale measurements of the abiotic environment
summary: One of the goals of ecological biogeography is to accurately predict where major vegetation types, such as forests or grasslands, can establish themselves. Alas, our current understanding of the mechanisms by which environmental variables jointly influence vegetation types does not allow for such predictions. Here, we compile a database of local measurements of soil, weather, topography, and bedrock lithology for 6404 sites across the continental United States, which we complement with information about the vegetation around the measurement sites. By applying machine learning methods to a subset of the sites, we are able to train a machine that predicts - using only information about abiotic variables - the presence of forests or grasslands with nearly 90% accuracy on the rest of the sites. We find that while weather variables are statistically important for these predictions, a few soil variables prove to be the most powerful predictors. By separating the combined contributions of weather and soil, we show that soil texture is a better predictor under dry conditions than under wet conditions, while pH is important predictor regardless of the weather. Furthermore, from 136 sites undergoing grassland-to-forest succession, our analysis indicates that soil pH changes with a certain lag relative to vegetation change. Sites that have recently undergone a transition exhibit a higher pH, closer to that of grasslands, despite the presence of trees. The pH then decreases by about one unit over a 30-year period of forest development. Ultimately, our results indicate that fine-scale environmental measurements and historical ecological data can serve as a basis for quantitative bio-geographical predictions, which could eventually guide targeted conservation interventions.

title: To mix or to de-mix?: Cation-π suppresses heterogeneity in local structure and dynamics of heterotypic Condensates
summary: Heterotypic biomolecular condensates can exhibit pronounced spatial and dynamic heterogeneity because chemically distinct components compete between self- and cross-association. Here, we use coarse-grained simulations to investigate how cation-{pi} interactions modulate this competition in condensates formed by peptides with systematic variation of hydrophobicity-to-charge ratios in binary peptide pairs. By independently tuning sequence heterogeneity, peptide composition, and cation-{pi} interaction strength, we establish how an additional short-range interaction reshapes condensate stability, internal organization, and molecular dynamics. In the absence of cation-{pi} interactions, highly heterogeneous peptide pairs form distinct core-shell architectures, with charge- and hydrophobicity-rich sequences preferentially occupying different regions of the condensate. Introducing cation-{pi} interactions progressively enhances phase stability and promotes molecular mixing, with stronger interactions substantially increasing the critical temperature and condensate density. Energetic analysis reveals that cation-{pi} interactions partially compensate for the loss of electrostatic and hydrophobic stabilization, providing an additional and tuneable source of cohesive interactions. This enhanced cross-association also suppresses spatial and dynamic heterogeneity, yielding more homogeneous peptide distributions, slower translational diffusion, and more uniform chain reconfiguration within the dense phase. Collectively, our results demonstrate that cation-{pi} interactions provide a molecular mechanism for coupling condensate stability to spatial organization and internal dynamics, enabling sequence heterogeneity and composition to be translated into distinct condensate states.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.

title: The (implicit) force is with you: an application of the implicit function theorem for automatic protein force fields reparametrization
summary: Molecular dynamics simulations are powerful tools for studying protein behavior, yet their accuracy remains limited by the approximations of molecular force fields and the difficulty of determining their parameters. Moreover, existing force fields are largely optimized for globular proteins and can perform poorly on structurally distinct systems. Developing a universal force field that accurately describes all existing protein structures may be beyond reach with current physical models. Instead, we propose shifting generality from the force field itself to the method used to assign its parameters, enabling systematic reparameterization for restricted, structurally homogeneous classes of proteins. We formulate this task as a bilevel optimization problem and solve it using the implicit function theorem. We demonstrate this approach by reparameterizing AMBER for amyloid fibrils, optimizing its parameters to improve agreement with experimentally determined structures and enhance fibril stability during molecular dynamics simulations.

title: Exploring the Upper Boundaries of Distance-Based Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction: Accuracy Improvements via Linear Regression and Artificial Neural Networks
summary: The traditional scoring functions for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction usually adopt fixed mathematical formulas to characterize atomic interaction energies, where electrostatic interactions are described by the a/r function and van der Waals interactions by the b/r^6 -c/r^12 function. These fixed power exponents of distance-based variables severely limit the predictive flexibility and generalization of conventional scoring models. To address this limitation, this study proposes an improved prediction strategy with unrestricted power exponents for distance-dependent atomic interaction variables. To explore the upper boundaries of the predictive powers, the optimized distance-based descriptors were integrated with linear regression and artificial neural network algorithms to construct novel models for protein-ligand binding affinity and binding energy prediction. All linear, artificial neural network, and hybrid models in this work were trained and validated on the latest high-quality dataset from PDBbind (version 2024). Quantitative evaluation based on the Pearson's correlation coefficient (R) demonstrated that the optimized linear models achieved a moderate predictive performance with R values ranging from 0.700 to 0.800 on the high-quality affinity dataset, while the artificial neural network-based hybrid models yielded substantially improved accuracy, with R values between 0.800 and 0.900. Comparative analysis verified that the optimal models established in this study outperform previously-reported state-of-the-art linear and machine learning-based scoring functions. Specially, this work indicates that the scoring functions with explicit mathematical expressions can achieve a high accuracy close to the experimental error for affinity prediction in a dataset composed of several thousand protein-ligand complexes. The overall results indicate that rationally-optimized power exponents for distance-based variables can effectively enhance the predictive accuracy of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction, providing a reliable and efficient tool for computational drug discovery.
